questions.q: What did Microsoft Defender for Cloud's posture dashboard flag on caldwelldocsstorage?
options: A high-severity finding that public blob access was enabled, exposing one container's contents with no authentication
A missing customer-managed key on the storage account
An expired TLS certificate on the storage endpoint
An overly permissive NSG rule on the storage account's subnet
questions.explain: The AllowBlobPublicAccess setting was enabled at the account level, and the invoices-shared container had public access set to Blob.

questions.q: How did Caldwell's team determine why and when the misconfiguration happened?
options: By reading the storage account's billing invoice
By filtering the Azure Activity Log for Set Storage Account Properties operations
By asking every employee individually if they made the change
There was no way to determine this after the fact
questions.explain: The Activity Log records control-plane changes, including who made them and when, which traced the change to a contractor three weeks earlier.

questions.q: Why does az storage account update --allow-blob-public-access false matter more than the container-level setting?
options: It permanently deletes the container
It has no real effect unless the container setting is also changed first
It only affects billing, not actual access
It is the account-level kill switch — once disabled, no container on that account can be public regardless of its own setting
questions.explain: AllowBlobPublicAccess at the account level gates whether any container-level public access setting can take effect at all.

questions.q: What should Caldwell use the next time someone outside the company needs one-off access to a file, instead of enabling public container access?
options: A permanent public container reserved just for that purpose
A new storage account with public access enabled by default
A time-limited SAS token scoped to that one blob
A shared admin password sent over email
questions.explain: A SAS token grants scoped, time-limited access to a single object without making anything publicly accessible to anyone with the URL indefinitely.

questions.q: Why does the team force a fresh Defender for Cloud assessment after remediating, instead of considering the fix complete once the CLI commands run?
options: The CLI commands do not actually take effect until a rescan is triggered
Defender for Cloud requires a manual rescan before any setting can be changed
Rescanning is only needed if the finding was low severity
Re-scanning confirms the resource actually shows as Healthy, rather than assuming the fix worked
questions.explain: Confirming the fix by re-scanning and verifying the Healthy status closes the loop instead of just assuming the remediation worked.
